Relative model of subpopulations and a reference population

Source: R/model-relative.R
relative_model.Rd

Joint model of subpopulations (for example deprivation quintiles) and the population they belong to (for example England): the relative model of Villegas and Haberman (2014, Section 2.4). The reference population has a Lee-Carter model, with a cohort effect if cohort = TRUE; each subpopulation's rates are the reference rates times an age pattern of level differences and an index of improvement differences. Section and equation numbers refer to that paper.

Usage

relative_model(
  reference,
  by = NULL,
  cohort = FALSE,
  deviation = c("mrwd", "rwd", "constant"),
  trend_from = NULL
)

Arguments

reference

The reference population: stratum labels, a named list of values of stratum variables (for example list(quintile = "England")), or an mt_data object (see Details).

by

Stratum variable(s) with a model each, for example "sex". NULL: one model for all strata.

cohort

Whether the reference model has cohort effects (eq. 16; the paper's "APC reference"). FALSE: Lee-Carter reference.

deviation

Forecast of the subpopulation indexes: "mrwd", "rwd" or "constant" (see Details).

trend_from

NULL (all years), or the first year of the reference index used for its random walk with drift.

Value

A model specification (joint over strata). The fit (fit$fits$models, one per group) holds the reference parameters (ref: alpha, beta, kappa, gamma and the time series parameters), the subpopulation parameters (alpha, beta, kappa, drift, sigma) and the log-likelihoods, effective numbers of parameters and BIC of both parts.

Model (Section 2.4, eqs. 16-18)

The reference rates are log mu'[x, t] = alpha'[x] + beta'[x] kappa'[t] + gamma'[t - x] (eq. 16), the age-period-cohort model of Renshaw and Haberman (2006) with cohort effects gamma'; with cohort = FALSE the cohort effects are left out and the reference has the Lee-Carter model (the paper's "LC reference"). The rates of subpopulation g are log mu[x, t, g] = log mubar[x, t] + alpha[x, g] + beta[x] kappa[t, g] (eq. 17). exp(alpha[x, g]) is the average ratio of the mortality of g to the reference (level differences); kappa[t, g] is the index of the improvements of g relative to the reference (a falling index: faster improvement), with the age pattern beta[x] common to all subpopulations. With beta[x] > 0, subpopulations keep their order as long as their indexes keep it (Section 2.4).

mubar[x, t] is the geometric mean of the reference rates over the single ages of the subpopulations' age group (eq. 18). The reference can cover more ages and years than the subpopulations (Section 2.4): the paper used England and Wales at ages 10-99 in 1961-2009 as the reference for English deprivation quintiles at ages 50-84 in 1981-2007.

Reference

reference is either

  • strata of the data: stratum labels or a named list of values of stratum variables, as in saint(), for example list(quintile = "England") after mt_aggregate_strata(). The reference strata of a group of by are pooled (sum of deaths and exposures) into one reference population. A single reference stratum of a group is forecast by the reference model; all other strata of the group are subpopulations. Reference and subpopulations then share ages and years, and mubar is the reference rate of the same age group;

  • an mt_data object with the reference population, which can cover more ages and years (Section 2.4). With by, its strata are matched to the groups of by by the values of these variables; the strata that match a group are pooled. Without by, all its strata are pooled into one reference. Every age group of the subpopulations must be a union of age groups of the reference, and every year of the subpopulations a year of the reference. All strata of the data are subpopulations. Preprocessing (mt_fit(prep = )) applies to the data, not to the reference.

Package-specific (reference unknown): where the reference has age groups wider than one year inside an age group of the subpopulations, mubar is their geometric mean weighted by the widths (eq. 18 for single ages); years of the reference after the last year of the data are not used, so that backtests use no later data (the paper's reference ends two years after its subpopulation data, Section 3).

Estimation (Sections 2.5 and 3.1)

Deaths of the reference and of the subpopulations are independent Poisson counts, and all parameters maximise the total log-likelihood (eq. 25), so the subpopulations also inform the reference parameters. The paper uses "straightforward extensions" of the Newton-Raphson procedure of Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt (2002). Here each iteration updates alpha', kappa', beta', gamma', alpha, kappa and beta in turn by one-dimensional Newton steps of the total log-likelihood, started from the Poisson Lee-Carter fit of the reference and a singular value decomposition of the subpopulations' log ratios to it. alpha' takes its steps from the reference deaths only: alpha[x, g] absorbs any change of alpha' in the subpopulation part, so its score there vanishes at the maximum and the steps reach the same maximum (package-specific). Package-specific (reference unknown): with cohort effects these iterations converge slowly, as known for this model (Section 2.5), and their fixed point is found with Anderson acceleration (Anderson 1965; Walker and Ni 2011), which extrapolates from the last ten iterations. The iterations stop when one iteration changes no fitted log rate by more than 1e-9 (at most 5,000 iterations; a warning of class mt_warning_relative_model otherwise). The fit reproduces StMoMo::rh(approxConst = TRUE) for a reference without subpopulations.

Constraints: sum(beta') = 1, sum(kappa') = 0, sum(gamma') = 0 over the cohorts (eqs. 19-21), sum(beta) = 1 and sum(kappa[, g]) = 0 for every g (eqs. 22-23). With cohort = TRUE, the cohort effects also have no linear trend, sum((c - cbar) gamma'[c]) = 0 (eq. 26), the approximate constraint of Hunt and Villegas (2015). It is imposed after every iteration by their approximately invariant transformation, as in StMoMo::rh(approxConst = TRUE) (Villegas, Kaishev and Millossovich 2018), the package of the first author: alpha', beta', kappa' and gamma' change so that the cohort effects lose their linear trend and the fitted rates stay the same where kappa' is linear. The transformation is skipped where kappa' has no trend (package-specific safeguard).

mt_parameters() reports, per part, the log-likelihood (with the log d! terms of eqs. 24-25), the effective number of parameters and the BIC of Section 3.1, L - 0.5 nu log N with N the number of cells (higher is better). The subpopulation part has nu = k m + k + n m - 1 - m parameters for k age groups, n years and m subpopulations, which gives the 171 of Table 1; the Lee-Carter reference has 2 k' + n' - 2 (227 in Table 1), the age-period-cohort reference 2 k' + n' + (k' + n' - 1) - 4, counting every cohort (363 for the dimensions of Table 1, which reports 353).

Forecasts (Sections 2.4 and 3.3)

Forecasts start from the fitted rates of the last year (eq. 32). The reference index kappa' follows a random walk with drift (Section 2.4); trend_from estimates it from the years from trend_from only, as the paper did with the years after 1980, where the index was close to linear (Section 3.3, following Haberman and Renshaw 2009). The subpopulation indexes follow, by deviation:

  • "mrwd": a multivariate random walk with drift with correlated normal innovations (eq. 4), the paper's model (Sections 2.4 and 3.3);

  • "rwd": independent random walks with drift (eq. 3). Section 2.1 notes that each subpopulation has the same forecast distribution under both processes, and that differences between subpopulations get wider intervals from independent walks; Section 3.1 compares both in a backtest (for the independent Lee-Carter model). With the same seed, the draws of the first subpopulation of a group are identical for both;

  • "constant": the indexes stay at their values of the last year, so all subpopulations improve as the reference (Scenario 2 of Section 3.4, eq. 33: level differences only).

The drifts are the mean year-to-year changes and the innovation (co)variances those of the changes around them, with divisor the number of changes minus one (as StMoMo::mrwd()). Draws include the innovations only: parameters, drifts and covariances are fixed, as in the paper, whose intervals "ignore any provision for parameter uncertainty" (Section 3.1). The reference index and the subpopulation indexes are independent, separate time series models as in the paper. Each group of by (for example each sex) is a separate model, as the paper fits women and men separately. Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates.

The drifting indexes let gaps between subpopulations widen or narrow without limit; li_lee(), coherent_fdm() and saint() keep the deviations from a common trend stationary.

Cohort effects: forecasts need no cohort beyond the fitted ones while the horizon is at most the distance between the youngest age of the subpopulations and the youngest age of the reference (the paper's case, Section 2.4). Later cohorts follow an ARIMA(1,1,0) model with drift of the fitted cohort effects, drawn with its innovations (package-specific: the paper does not extrapolate cohorts; this is the default of StMoMo::forecast.fitStMoMo()).

Data

The reference needs single-year consecutive ages without an open interval for cohort = TRUE (the paper uses single ages, Section 3), positive exposures, and deaths at every age (and in every cohort). Subpopulations need deaths in every age group and every year.

References

Villegas AM, Haberman S (2014). On the modeling and forecasting of socioeconomic mortality differentials: an application to deprivation and mortality in England. North American Actuarial Journal 18(1): 168-193. doi:10.1080/10920277.2013.866034

Renshaw AE, Haberman S (2006). A cohort-based extension to the Lee-Carter model for mortality reduction factors. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 38(3): 556-570. doi:10.1016/j.insmatheco.2005.12.001

Hunt A, Villegas AM (2015). Robustness and convergence in the Lee-Carter model with cohort effects. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 64: 186-202. doi:10.1016/j.insmatheco.2015.05.004

Brouhns N, Denuit M, Vermunt JK (2002). A Poisson log-bilinear regression approach to the construction of projected lifetables. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 31(3): 373-393. doi:10.1016/S0167-6687(02)00185-3

Haberman S, Renshaw A (2009). On age-period-cohort parametric mortality rate projections. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 45(2): 255-270. doi:10.1016/j.insmatheco.2009.07.006

Villegas AM, Kaishev VK, Millossovich P (2018). StMoMo: an R package for stochastic mortality modeling. Journal of Statistical Software 84(3): 1-38. doi:10.18637/jss.v084.i03

Anderson DG (1965). Iterative procedures for nonlinear integral equations. Journal of the ACM 12(4): 547-560. doi:10.1145/321296.321305

Walker HF, Ni P (2011). Anderson acceleration for fixed-point iterations. SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 49(4): 1715-1735. doi:10.1137/10078356X

See also

saint(), another model of populations relative to a reference; cae(), whose populations also keep drifting indexes.

Examples

x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"),
             age = "age_group", value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)),
                     name = "quintile")
x <- mt_subset(x, ages = c(50, 85))
xa <- mt_aggregate_strata(x, mt_hierarchy(quintile = list(total = "England")))
fit <- mt_fit(relative_model(reference = list(quintile = "England"), by = "sex"), xa)
p <- mt_parameters(fit)
p[parameter == "bic"]
#>                  stratum parameter  index     value
#>                   <char>    <char> <char>     <num>
#> 1:      reference female       bic        -1062.329
#> 2: subpopulations female       bic        -4076.166
#> 3:        reference male       bic        -1197.945
#> 4:   subpopulations male       bic        -4268.884
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
